title: Talking about exceptions
subtitle: except (for) / besides / apart from / but for
summary: Say what a statement leaves out with except (for), apart from and but, add to it with besides, and imagine a different past with but for.

lesson.heading: except (for)
lesson.text: We use **except (for)** to introduce the only thing or person that a statement does not include. Straight before a noun or pronoun, both forms are possible.

examples.text: The price of the holiday includes all meals **except (for)** lunch.
Everyone seemed to have been invited **except (for)** Mrs Woodford and me.
I had no money to give him **except (for)** the few coins in my pocket.

lesson.heading: except, not except for
lesson.text: We use **except** on its own before to-infinitives, bare infinitives, prepositions and that-clauses - including those where *that* is left out.

examples.text: I rarely need to go into the city centre **except to do** some shopping.
They look just like the real thing, **except (that)** they're made of plastic.
There is likely to be rain everywhere today **except in** Wales.
There is nothing more the doctor can do **except keep** an eye on him.

lesson.note: Informally you will hear except for in these places too, but it is not considered grammatically correct.

lesson.heading: Taking away or adding on?

left.label: except (for) - not included
examples: I don't enjoy watching any sports **except (for)** cricket. (= I enjoy only cricket)
I haven't read anything by her, **except (for)** one of her short stories.

right.label: besides - as well as, in addition to
examples: **Besides** cricket, I enjoy watching football and basketball. (= I enjoy three sports)
**Besides** her novels and poems, she published a number of short stories.

lesson.note: Apart from does both jobs: I don't enjoy watching any sports apart from cricket. (= except for) / Apart from cricket, I enjoy watching football and basketball. (= besides)

lesson.heading: but after negative words
lesson.text: After negative words such as **no**, **nobody** and **nothing** we can use **but** with a meaning close to except (for).

examples.text: After the operation he could see nothing **but** / **except (for)** / **apart from** vague shadows.
There was no way out **but** / **except** / **apart from** upwards, towards the light.

lesson.heading: but for - a past that did not happen
lesson.text: **But for** means something quite different. We use it to say what would or might have happened if the thing it introduces had not happened.

examples.text: The country would now be self-sufficient in food **but for** the drought last year.
examples.note: = if there hadn't been the drought ...

examples.text: **But for** the leg injury he suffered last year, he would probably have been picked for the national team by now.
examples.note: = if he hadn't injured his leg ...

lesson.note: In informal speech some people use except for in this way too: I'd have got there on time except for / but for the taxi being late.

lesson.heading: excepted, apart, aside
lesson.text: After mentioning a person or thing, we can add **excepted**, **apart** or **aside** to show that they are not included in the statement we make.

examples.text: It has been, 1984 **excepted** / **apart** / **aside**, the hottest July for the last 100 years.

lesson.text: except (for) subtracts, besides adds, and but for imagines a past that did not happen.

exercises.prompt: I liked everything in the meal ___ the cabbage.
exercises.explanation: Straight before a noun, both except and except for are possible.

exercises.prompt: After the operation he could see nothing ___ vague shadows.
exercises.explanation: After a negative word like nothing, but means the same as except (for).

exercises.prompt: She had no choice ___ to wait for the next train.
exercises.explanation: Before a to-infinitive we use except, never except for.

exercises.statement: Besides being small, Denmark is very flat, with villages linked by country roads.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Besides here means 'as well as' - it adds a second fact about Denmark.

exercises.prompt: I had nothing to do ___ sit by the pool and relax.
exercises.explanation: Before a bare infinitive (sit) we use except.

exercises.statement: She had never been out of the country besides a week in Ireland as a child.
exercises.explanation: She had never been out of the country except for a week in Ireland as a child. The week in Ireland is the one exception, not an addition.

exercises.prompt: Does the sentence leave something out or add something on?

items.text: I don't enjoy watching any sports except for cricket.
Besides cricket, I enjoy watching football and basketball.
I haven't read anything by her, except for one of her short stories.
Besides her novels and poems, she published a number of short stories.
There was nothing in the fridge except for a rather mouldy piece of cheese.
Besides being small, Denmark is very flat.

exercises.prompt: He gave no excuse for turning up late ___ that he was tired.
exercises.explanation: Before a that-clause we use except.

exercises.statement: Except for his novels, Campbell wrote a number of biographies.
exercises.explanation: Besides his novels, Campbell wrote a number of biographies. The biographies are in addition to the novels, so we need besides.

exercises.prompt: ___ the problems with my computer, I would have got the book finished weeks ago.
exercises.explanation: But for says what would have happened if the problems had not occurred.

exercises.prompt: Match each but for phrase with what would have happened without it.

pairs.left: But for the excellent directions Katerina gave me,
pairs.right: I would have got totally lost.

pairs.left: But for the interruptions caused by the bad weather,
pairs.right: the building would have been completed by now.

pairs.left: But for the food and medicines supplied by the charity,
pairs.right: many more people would have died in the famine.

pairs.left: But for the shelter provided by the trees,
pairs.right: the wind would have caused even more damage to the house.

pairs.left: But for the threat of sanctions by the EU,
pairs.right: human rights would not have improved in the country.

pairs.left: But for the loan from the bank,
pairs.right: I would not have been able to set up my business.

exercises.prompt: The bad weather caused interruptions, so the building is still not finished. Say it with But for the ... .
exercises.answer: But for the interruptions caused by the bad weather, the building would have been completed by now.
exercises.explanation: But for + noun phrase replaces a whole if-clause: if the bad weather had not caused interruptions ...
